But as we can see game theory outlined in The Prisoner's Dilemma, when everyone is cooperating, there is an opportunity for bad actors to take advantage of others' cooperation for their own short term gain

If you aren't familiar with the thought experiment of The Prisoner's Dilemma, it is fundamentally an experiment to understand the incentives around cooperative behavior.

The basic idea is that two robbers are caught trespassing, but the cops don't have enough evidence to convict them of the more serious crime of stealing. If they both remain silent, they both get a small penalty for the trespassing. However, they are given the option to rat the other robber out, condemning them to a much longer prison sentence, in exchange for going free. 

From a pure game theory perspective, if you know the other party will stay silent, it is strictly better for you to rat them out and get off free and so both robbers are actually incentivized to rat, even though it's better over all if they cooperate.

What is so interesting about this is that if you run this experiment in the real world, people will often default to cooperation. This decision baffled game theorists and sparked a large effort to explain why so many people were making this suboptimal decision to cooperate.

What game theorists found is if you add the element of time, that is to say you have the same people repeat the experiment an indefinite number of times, the game theory optimal solution changes to mutual cooperation. This makes perfect sense. You can take advantage of someone's cooperation in the short term, but they probably aren't going to cooperate with you (let alone play with you) again.

So scientist think that because people default to thinking of the repetitive nature of cooperative decisions, even when asked to play only once, test participants will typically choose to cooperate despite the fact that game theory says they shouldn't.

This has further interesting implications when you play with people who can't think into the future, but that is a whole other matter entirely...

Because of this danger of one's cooperation being taken advantage of, the best strategy when playing the Prisoner's Dilemma is called Tit for Tat

Start by cooperating then mirror whatever your opponent does. This facilitates the ideal equilibrium of cooperation while punishing any non cooperative behavior and allowing forgiveness

The story of how Tit for Tat was discovered is also fascinating. Sparked by the seeming contradiction in people's preference to cooperate in The Prisoner's Dilemma despite game theory saying otherwise, there was a programming competition held to see which strategy could achieve the best individual results.

Programmers created algorithms and pitted them against each other to see which one performed best. Interestingly enough, it wasn't a complicated strategy that won. Nor was it a strategy that took advantage of its opponents. Tit for Tat won because it balanced incentivizing cooperation while refusing to allow itself to be taken advantage of. It didn't perform better than if both sides had only cooperated, but it performed the least worst in an environment where all strategies wanted to win and weren't shy about not cooperating to do it.

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand traces the evolution of the 'super-cooperator cluster' concept from aspirational vision (Visa's 2020 'golden age' meme) through theoretical grounding (Andres's Dec 2021 coinage of the term, anchored in game theory and MDMA-consciousness speculation) to practical instantiation attempts (Dan Allison's 2023 tooling efforts, MetaPrime's 2024 contextual morality framework) and finally to memetic crystallization (2025 comic book visualization). The boundary object is the phrase itself—'super-cooperator cluster'—which functions as both descriptor and召唤 incantation. The arc is constructive rather than dialectical: each node adds layers (aspiration→theory→praxis→mythology) without fundamental contradiction. However, the strand suffers from 'vaporware syndrome': lots of pointing at the thing, minimal evidence of the thing actually coordinating at scale.

essential_tweets.annotation: The Origin Meme: Visa's 2020 COVID-era vision of 'friendly ambitious nerds' building toward a 'golden age'—the aspirational substrate before the concept had a name.
The Naming: Andres coins 'super-cooperator cluster' (Dec 2021), grounding it in game theory and speculative neuroscience (MDMA-consciousness as political fuel).
Visa's Endorsement: The seed tweet—Visa quote-tweets Andres 1.5 years later, validating the concept and injecting it into his high-follower network.
Pre-Context: Rich Decibels' 2021 analysis of M_ashcroft's Alexander Technique business as example of 'infinity integrity' cooperator—shows the cluster's proto-members already operating.
The Failure Mode: Loopholekid's 2021 thread on why cooperatives fail (bad faith actors, ego, insufficient shared understanding)—the cautionary tale the cluster must avoid.
The Tooling Attempt: Dan Allison's 2023 effort to build infrastructure (Decisive Team, Discourse, OpenCollective) for spontaneous self-organization—praxis meets the theory.
The Moral Framework: MetaPrime's 'Batman Delusion' thread (April 2024) on contextual morality and Tit-for-Tat—providing the ethical substrate for discriminating cooperators from defectors.

The Belief Declaration: Nosilverv's viral tweet (April 2025) expressing faith that the cluster exists and is discoverable—shifting from 'we should build this' to 'it already exists, I just need to find it.'
The Immanence Claim: AngularOcean's reply asserting 'we are in it right now'—the cluster recognizing itself, the acausal handshake completing.
The Mythologization: Nosilverv's AI-generated comic book concept (April 2025)—the idea becoming self-aware enough to imagine its own propaganda, closing the loop from aspiration to legend.

title: The “Super-Cooperator Cluster” goes full myth mode
summary: It peaks when people try to make it real and then when it gets memed into legend. @danallison becomes the resident infrastructure guy: he riffs on naming (“SCC?”), pitches “The Good Internet,” and in 2023 drops a concrete plan—spontaneous movements fail because they can’t decide/act fast (citing @zeynep’s *Twitter and Tear Gas*), so you need tools for the OODA loop: Twitter for Observe, @discourse for Orient, @DecisiveTeam_ for Decide, @opencollect for Act. Meanwhile @MetaPrime001 provides the ethical boundary layer: cooperation works until “Toxic Tolerance” lets defectors farm you, so adopt Tit‑for‑Tat / “minimal necessary force.” By 2025 the discourse kind of stops being about building anything and starts being about *recognizing* you’re already in it: @nosilverv goes viral with “I’ll know how to join them,” @AngularOcean replies “we are in it right now,” and @nosilverv caps it with an AI-generated comic book (“THE SOCIETY OF HYPER‑COOPERATORS”)—the concept becomes self-aware enough to make propaganda. Why care: it’s a live case study in how internet subcultures turn a coordination wish into a boundary object and then into a quasi-religion—plus the uncomfortable question hanging over it is @loopholekid’s: cool myth, but can it survive contact with ego, defectors, and real-world scale?
